title: Keevash–Mubayi–Sudakov–Verstraëte Question on Rainbow Cycles
statement_text: What is the maximum possible average degree of a properly edge-coloured graph on $n$ vertices containing no rainbow cycle?
context_text: Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov, and Verstraëte raised this question in 2007 as a rainbow analogue of the classical fact that average degree at least 2 guarantees a cycle. The lower bound $\Omega(\log n)$ was already established in [39]; prior to this paper the best upper bound was $O(\log^2 n)$, due independently to Janzer–Sudakov and Kim–Lee–Liu–Tran.
paper_contribution: Proves an upper bound of $(\log n)^{1+o(1)}$ on the maximum average degree, matching the $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound up to the $o(1)$ term in the exponent and essentially resolving the question.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

title: Question 10.1
statement_text: Is the $\log\log n$ factor necessary in order to guarantee a rainbow cycle, in the theorem that there exists $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle? That is, does average degree $C\log n$ suffice?
context_text: An edge-colouring is proper if the edges at each vertex have distinct colours, and a subgraph is rainbow if no colour appears on more than one of its edges; $d(G)$ is the average degree and logarithms are natural. Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov and Verstraëte asked how large the average degree of a properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph must be to guarantee a rainbow cycle; they showed that $\Omega(\log n)$ is needed, still the best lower bound, and upper bounds improved from $O(n^{1/3})$ through $e^{(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$, $O(\log^4n)$ and $(\log n)^{2+o(1)}$ to $O(\log^2n)$. The authors prove that there is $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle, tight up to the $\log\log n$ factor. The proof first passes to a robust sublinear expander subgraph and then randomly splits the colour palette into two parts, showing that most vertices are reachable by rainbow walks in each part; this approach needs the $\log\log n$ term, since there are properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expanders (built from Hamming graphs) with average degree $\log n(\log\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ in which random colour subsampling with probability $\frac12$ leaves no large component w.h.p. The authors view this as circumstantial evidence that the factor might be needed, and note that the transposition question ($t(k)$ for $\mathcal{S}_k$) might help decide it.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

title: Question 10.2
statement_text: Does there exist a constant $C>0$ such that the edges of any $n$-vertex properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expander $G$ with average degree at least $C\log n$ can be decomposed into two spanning connected subgraphs in such a way that every colour appears on only one of them?
context_text: An edge-colouring is proper if the edges at each vertex have distinct colours, and a subgraph is rainbow if no colour appears on more than one of its edges; $d(G)$ is the average degree and logarithms are natural. Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov and Verstraëte asked how large the average degree of a properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph must be to guarantee a rainbow cycle; they showed that $\Omega(\log n)$ is needed, still the best lower bound, and upper bounds improved from $O(n^{1/3})$ through $e^{(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$, $O(\log^4n)$ and $(\log n)^{2+o(1)}$ to $O(\log^2n)$. The authors prove that there is $C>0$ such that every properly edge-coloured graph on $n\ge3$ vertices with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ contains a rainbow cycle, tight up to the $\log\log n$ factor. A graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is a robust sublinear expander if for every $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, every non-empty $U\subseteq V(G)$ with $|U|\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$ and every set $F$ of at most $(\varepsilon/3)\,d(G)\,|U|$ edges, the neighbourhood of $U$ in $G-F$ (vertices outside $U$ adjacent to $U$) has size at least $(\varepsilon/3)|U|$. Every graph contains a robust sublinear expander subgraph $H$ with $d(H)/\log|V(H)|$ comparable to $d(G)/\log|V(G)|$. The most natural approach, assigning each colour independently with probability $\frac12$ to one of the two subgraphs, fails: there are properly edge-coloured robust sublinear expanders of average degree $\log n(\log\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ (from Hamming graphs) for which both resulting subgraphs are disconnected w.h.p. A positive answer would not quite suffice to remove the $\log\log n$ factor from the rainbow-cycle theorem; what would suffice is a pair of vertices joined by rainbow paths in both subgraphs, which would follow if the two subgraphs were (weaker) robust sublinear expanders rather than just connected.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

title: Question 10.3
statement_text: Given a positive integer $n$, what is the smallest number $d=d(n)$ so that in any group $G$ of size $|G|=n$, given any subset $S\subseteq G$ of size $|S|\geq d$, we can always find a solution to $g_{1}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdot\ldots\cdot g_{m}^{\varepsilon_{m}}=e$ with distinct $g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}\in S$ as well as $\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{m}\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\geq 1$.
context_text: For a group $(G,\cdot)$ with identity $e$, a subset $S$ is dissociated if there is no solution to $g_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots g_m^{\varepsilon_m}=e$ with distinct $g_i\in S$, $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\ge1$; the additive dimension $\dim A$ of a finite set $A$ is the largest size of a dissociated subset of $A$, and $\dim G$ equals the plus-minus weighted Davenport constant $D_\pm(G)$. A Cayley-graph argument links this to rainbow cycles, and the rainbow-cycle theorem gives $\dim A=O(K\log|A|\log\log|A|)$ whenever $|A\cdot A|\le K|A|$ (a non-abelian version of Sanders' theorem $\dim A=O(K\log|A|)$ for abelian groups), hence $\dim G=O(\log|G|\log\log|G|)$ for every finite group with $|G|\ge3$; for abelian groups $\dim G\le\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$, which fails for non-abelian groups since $\dim\mathcal{S}_3^k\ge\frac{3}{\log_26}\log_2|\mathcal{S}_3^k|$. Equivalently, $d(n)-1$ is the maximum of $\dim G=D_\pm(G)$ over groups of order $n$. The authors' bound gives $d(n)\le O(\log n\log\log n)$, and $d(n)\ge\Omega(\log n)$ is easy; it is unclear whether the $\log\log n$ factor is necessary. The case $G=\mathcal{S}_k$ is of particular interest, since every $k$-element group embeds in $\mathcal{S}_k$ and the best lower bounds on $d(n)$ come from dissociated sets of transpositions. This question is not about graphs, but it is connected to rainbow cycles in properly edge-coloured Cayley graphs.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings

title: Question 10.4
statement_text: Given $k\geq 2$, determine the minimum number $t=t(k)$ such that any set of $t$ transpositions in $\mathcal{S}_{k}$ contains a non-empty subset whose elements can be multiplied in some order to give the identity.
context_text: $\mathcal{S}_k$ is the symmetric group on $k$ elements. Equivalently, $t(k)-1$ is the additive dimension of the set of all transpositions of $\mathcal{S}_k$, i.e. the largest size of a set of transpositions with no non-empty subset whose elements multiply, in some order, to the identity; since a transposition is its own inverse, this is the same as being dissociated (no solution to $g_1^{\pm1}\cdots g_m^{\pm1}=e$ with distinct $g_i$). For a group $(G,\cdot)$ with identity $e$, a subset $S$ is dissociated if there is no solution to $g_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots g_m^{\varepsilon_m}=e$ with distinct $g_i\in S$, $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and $m\ge1$; the additive dimension $\dim A$ of a finite set $A$ is the largest size of a dissociated subset of $A$, and $\dim G$ equals the plus-minus weighted Davenport constant $D_\pm(G)$. A Cayley-graph argument links this to rainbow cycles, and the rainbow-cycle theorem gives $\dim A=O(K\log|A|\log\log|A|)$ whenever $|A\cdot A|\le K|A|$ (a non-abelian version of Sanders' theorem $\dim A=O(K\log|A|)$ for abelian groups), hence $\dim G=O(\log|G|\log\log|G|)$ for every finite group with $|G|\ge3$; for abelian groups $\dim G\le\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$, which fails for non-abelian groups since $\dim\mathcal{S}_3^k\ge\frac{3}{\log_26}\log_2|\mathcal{S}_3^k|$. The authors show $k(\log k)^{1-o(1)}\le t(k)\le O(k(\log k)^2)$; the upper bound comes from applying the rainbow-cycle theorem (every properly edge-coloured $n$-vertex graph with average degree at least $C\log n\log\log n$ has a rainbow cycle) to a Cayley graph on $k!$ vertices, where $\log\log(k!)$ costs a factor $\log k$, while earlier rainbow-cycle bounds gave nothing better than the trivial $t(k)\le\binom{k}{2}$. These transposition sets give the best known lower bounds for the maximum additive dimension of groups of order $n$, and the question might help decide whether the $\log\log n$ factor is needed in the rainbow-cycle theorem.
paper_title: Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings
